scenes.visual: Title card 'Count the Working Sites' fades in over a cartoon slice of raw potato beside a brown drugstore bottle labelled 'hydrogen peroxide'. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. COLOUR MAP, the same in every scene and in the second film: ENZYME = BLUE rounded block with a notch cut in one side (the notch is the active site), drawn like the lesson's enzyme-cycle figure; SUBSTRATE = ORANGE (a small ORANGE wedge that fits the notch in film 1; ORANGE bead strings for gelatin chains in film 2); PRODUCTS = GREEN; DENATURED ENZYME = GREY bent block whose notch no longer matches the ORANGE shape; WORKING SITES = BLUE counter, top left, reading 'working sites: n of 8'; SPEED PER SITE = YELLOW needle gauge, top right; RATE = PURPLE bar, bottom right, whose height is always the counter times the gauge. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Drop a slice of raw potato into hydrogen peroxide, and it fizzes. Something in the potato does the work, so why is it never used up? Hydrogen peroxide breaks down alone, but slowly. The bubbles are oxygen gas.
scenes.visual: The potato slice drops into a glass of clear liquid labelled 'hydrogen peroxide'. Bubbles stream up and a foam head grows while the narrator speaks. A side glass with no potato shows one bubble every few seconds, labelled 'no potato: slow'. A large question mark hovers over the potato: 'used up?'
scenes.narration: Drop a slice of raw potato into hydrogen peroxide, and it fizzes. Something in the potato does the work, so why is it never used up? Hydrogen peroxide breaks down alone, but slowly. The bubbles are oxygen gas.

scenes.tts: The worker is catalase, an enzyme found in potato cells, liver cells and many others. An enzyme is a molecule, almost always a protein, that speeds up a specific reaction.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the potato: cartoon cells, then one BLUE block with a notch, labelled 'catalase (an enzyme)'. A small cartoon liver beside the potato also lights up with BLUE blocks. A word equation writes itself along the bottom: 'hydrogen peroxide → water + oxygen', with 'hydrogen peroxide' in ORANGE and 'water + oxygen' in GREEN.
scenes.narration: The worker is catalase, an enzyme found in potato cells, liver cells and many others. An enzyme is a molecule, almost always a protein, that speeds up a specific reaction.

scenes.tts: Follow one catalase. Its substrate, the molecule it acts on, is hydrogen peroxide. The substrate drifts into the active site, a small pocket on the enzyme. There it is turned into products, water and oxygen. The products leave, and the enzyme is unchanged.
scenes.visual: One large BLUE block with its notch labelled 'active site'. Two ORANGE wedges labelled 'substrate: hydrogen peroxide' drift in one after the other and sit in the notch in turn. Between them they leave as three GREEN pieces labelled '2 water + 1 oxygen', which float away. A small on-screen equation reads '2 hydrogen peroxide → 2 water + oxygen'. The BLUE block is left exactly as it started; a faint outline of its starting shape overlays it to show nothing changed.
scenes.narration: Follow one catalase. Its substrate, the molecule it acts on, is hydrogen peroxide. The substrate drifts into the active site, a small pocket on the enzyme. There it is turned into products, water and oxygen. The products leave, and the enzyme is unchanged.

scenes.tts: Then it takes in the next one, and the next. The same enzyme works again and again. That makes it a catalyst, a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
scenes.visual: The cycle from the last scene repeats faster and faster with new ORANGE wedges arriving. A tally in the corner counts 'molecules changed: 1, 2, 3, ... 40, 41' and keeps running. The BLUE block never changes size or colour. Label appears under it: 'catalyst: not used up'.
scenes.narration: Then it takes in the next one, and the next. The same enzyme works again and again. That makes it a catalyst, a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

scenes.tts: Why does this pocket take only hydrogen peroxide? The active site's shape and electric charges fit only certain molecules. So each enzyme usually speeds up one reaction, or a few similar ones.
scenes.visual: Three shapes approach the BLUE notch: the ORANGE wedge, a round shape and a long shape (both outlined in black, unlabelled except 'other molecules'). Only the ORANGE wedge slides in. Small plus and minus marks appear along the notch's edge and matching marks on the wedge, lighting up as they line up. Label: 'shape and charges fit'.
scenes.narration: Why does this pocket take only hydrogen peroxide? The active site's shape and electric charges fit only certain molecules. So each enzyme usually speeds up one reaction, or a few similar ones.

scenes.tts: And why does fitting make the reaction faster? Picture a ball that must be pushed over a hill before it rolls down the other side. Activation energy is the energy needed to get a reaction started, like that hill. An enzyme does not add energy. It lowers the hill.
scenes.visual: A side-on energy graph labelled 'schematic': an ORANGE ball on the left, a tall hump in the middle, a lower valley on the right where the ball turns GREEN. The hump is labelled 'activation energy'. Balls jiggle and only rarely one crosses. Then a BLUE outline slides under the hump and the hump sinks to half its height; no energy is added to the ball (a crossed-out lightning bolt flashes by the ball).
scenes.narration: And why does fitting make the reaction faster? Picture a ball that must be pushed over a hill before it rolls down the other side. Activation energy is the energy needed to get a reaction started, like that hill. An enzyme does not add energy. It lowers the hill.

scenes.tts: With a lower hill, many more molecules cross each second. The hill is a graph of energy, not a real place.
scenes.visual: The same graph with the low hump. Now a stream of ORANGE balls crosses and turns GREEN on the far side; a crossings-per-second counter beside it jumps from a slow tick to a fast blur. A small caption tag appears on the graph: 'a graph, not a place'.
scenes.narration: With a lower hill, many more molecules cross each second. The hill is a graph of energy, not a real place.

scenes.tts: Now pull back to eight active sites, one per block. Two things set how fast the tube makes products. First, how many active sites are working, still in the shape that fits. Second, the speed of each site: how much product it makes per second.
scenes.visual: Pull back to a cartoon test tube with eight BLUE blocks floating among ORANGE wedges. The BLUE counter appears top left: 'working sites: 8 of 8'. The YELLOW gauge appears top right: 'speed per site', needle at the middle. A small label under the blocks reads 'simplified: one block = one active site'. Each block flashes as it finishes a cycle.
scenes.narration: Now pull back to eight active sites, one per block. Two things set how fast the tube makes products. First, how many active sites are working, still in the shape that fits. Second, the speed of each site: how much product it makes per second.

scenes.tts: The rate is the two multiplied together: working sites times the speed of each site. A site makes product only while a substrate sits in it. So temperature, P H and the amount of substrate each turn one dial, or both.
scenes.caption: The rate is the two multiplied together: working sites times the speed of each site. A site makes product only while a substrate sits in it. So temperature, pH and the amount of substrate each turn one dial, or both.
scenes.visual: Between the counter and the gauge an equation builds: 'rate = working sites × speed of each site'. The PURPLE rate bar rises to match. One BLUE block empties for a moment and stops flashing until a new ORANGE wedge arrives. Three small grey tags slide in underneath, unlit, reading 'temperature', 'pH' and 'substrate'; the 'substrate' tag's thin arrow points at the gauge, the others at both the counter and the gauge. No curves are shown.
scenes.narration: The rate is the two multiplied together: working sites times the speed of each site. A site makes product only while a substrate sits in it. So temperature, pH and the amount of substrate each turn one dial, or both.

scenes.tts: Suppose one active site is bent out of shape, so the substrate no longer fits. What happens to the counter, and to the rate?
scenes.visual: One of the eight BLUE blocks turns GREY and bends; its notch no longer matches the ORANGE wedges, which bounce off it. The counter and the bar freeze with a question mark over each.
scenes.narration: Suppose one active site is bent out of shape, so the substrate no longer fits. What happens to the counter, and to the rate?

scenes.visual: Hold the frozen tube. A small 5-second timer ring fills in the corner. On-screen text: 'Predict: counter? rate bar?'

scenes.tts: The counter drops to seven of eight. That site is not working, so the rate bar shrinks by an eighth. The other seven sites run just as fast as before.
scenes.visual: The counter ticks from 'working sites: 8 of 8' to '7 of 8'. The PURPLE bar drops; a bracket marks the missing top slice '1/8 of the rate'. The YELLOW gauge needle does not move, and a tick mark beside it reads 'speed per site: unchanged'. The seven BLUE blocks keep flashing at the same pace.
scenes.narration: The counter drops to seven of eight. That site is not working, so the rate bar shrinks by an eighth. The other seven sites run just as fast as before.

scenes.tts: A site bent so far that the substrate no longer fits does not work slowly. It does not work at all. Anything that bends active sites out of shape lowers the count.
scenes.visual: Side by side: a GREY bent block with an ORANGE wedge bouncing off (label 'not working'), and a BLUE block cycling (label 'working'). Then both dials zoom to the centre beside the PURPLE bar and the equation, and hold.
scenes.narration: A site bent so far that the substrate no longer fits does not work slowly. It does not work at all. Anything that bends active sites out of shape lowers the count.

scenes.visual: End card with the hexagon mascot holding a small BLUE notched block. Line: 'Rate = working active sites × speed of each site.'
